proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  By \(\mathrm{def:exact\mbox{-}model}\), all of its member assumptions hold.  For \(a\in\{0,1\}\), define
\[
p_a(x)=a e_P(x)+(1-a)\{1-e_P(x)\}.
\]
The propensity-normalization and propensity-envelope assumptions give
\[
\frac14\le p_1(x)=e_P(x)\le\frac12,
\qquad
\frac12\le p_0(x)=1-e_P(x)\le\frac34
\quad (x\in\mathcal X).
\]
In particular, both \(p_a\) are everywhere strictly positive; this is the condition used below when dividing by treatment probabilities.

Let \(m_a(X)\) be any version of \(\mathbb E_P[Y(a)\mid\sigma(X)]\).  Such a version is integrable because \(Y(a)\in\{0,1\}\).  For every bounded Borel function \(q:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), consistency gives
\[
\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y=\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y(a)
\quad P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
Consequently, the defining identity for conditional expectation and then conditional exchangeability yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y\right]
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y(a)\right] \\
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbb E_P\!\left\{\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y(a)\mid X\right\}\right] \\
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbb E_P\!\left\{\mathbf 1\{A=a\}\mid X\right\}
                         \mathbb E_P\!\left\{Y(a)\mid X\right\}\right] \\
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)p_a(X)m_a(X)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the third equality is precisely the conditional factorization supplied by \(\mathrm{ass:conditional\mbox{-}exchangeability}\), applied to \(Y(a)\), and the last equality follows from the definition of \(e_P\) and of \(m_a\).

On the other hand, the definition of the observed conditional regression \(\mu_{a,P}\) and two applications of the tower property give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}Y\right]
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}
       \mathbb E_P\!\left\{Y\mid X,A\right\}\right] \\
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\mathbf 1\{A=a\}\mu_{a,P}(X)\right] \\
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)p_a(X)\mu_{a,P}(X)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Comparing the last two displays shows that
\[
\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)p_a(X)\{\mu_{a,P}(X)-m_a(X)\}\right]=0
\]
for every bounded Borel \(q\).  Taking \(q(X)\) to be the sign of
\(p_a(X)\{\mu_{a,P}(X)-m_a(X)\}\) gives
\[
\mathbb E_P\!\left[
  \left|p_a(X)\{\mu_{a,P}(X)-m_a(X)\}\right|
\right]=0.
\]
The strict lower bounds on \(p_a\) therefore imply
\[
\mu_{a,P}(X)=m_a(X)
\quad P\text{-almost surely},\qquad a\in\{0,1\}.
\]
By the definition \(\tau_P=\mu_{1,P}-\mu_{0,P}\), it follows that
\[
\tau_P(X)=m_1(X)-m_0(X)
\quad P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
Moreover, for every bounded Borel \(q\), linearity of ordinary expectation and the defining identities for \(m_1,m_0\) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\{m_1(X)-m_0(X)\}\right]
&=\mathbb E_P[q(X)Y(1)]-\mathbb E_P[q(X)Y(0)] \\
&=\mathbb E_P\!\left[q(X)\{Y(1)-Y(0)\}\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(m_1-m_0\) is a version of \(\mathbb E_P[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X]\), proving
\[
\tau_P(x)=\mathbb E_P[Y(1)-Y(0)\mid X=x]
\quad\text{for }P_X\text{-almost every }x.
\]

It remains to justify the endpoint assertion, rather than assign a value to a null-event conditional mean by convention.  The contrast-H\"older assumption and the definition of \(\mathcal H_d^\gamma(L)\) imply that \(\tau_P\) is continuous on \(\mathcal X\): for H\"older order at most one this is the stated H\"older condition on the function itself, and for larger order it follows from the existence of the bounded first derivatives in that definition.  The preceding almost-everywhere equality says that \(\tau_P\) is a continuous version of the causal conditional mean.

To prove uniqueness, let \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) be any other continuous version.  If \(f(x_0)\ne\tau_P(x_0)\) at some \(x_0\in\mathcal X\), continuity of \(f-\tau_P\) supplies a relative open neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_0\) on which
\[
|f(x)-\tau_P(x)|>\frac12|f(x_0)-\tau_P(x_0)|>0.
\]
Every nonempty relative open neighborhood in \([0,1]^d\) contains a positive-volume axis-aligned rectangle.  Hence the uniform-design assumption implies \(P_X(U)>0\), contradicting equality of the two versions \(P_X\)-almost everywhere.  Therefore \(f=\tau_P\) on all of \(\mathcal X\).  In particular, the uniquely determined continuous version at the boundary point \(0\) is \(\tau_P(0)\), as claimed.

Fix \(P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), and abbreviate \(e=e_P\), \(\mu_0=\mu_{0,P}\), and \(\tau=\tau_P\).  All constants below are uniform in \(P\) and may depend only on \((d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  Put \(D_0=[0,1]^d\), \(h=h_n\), \(M=M_n\), \(K=K_n\), and \(\ell=h/M\).  Let \(\Pi_M\) denote coordinatewise Lebesgue orthogonal projection on the piecewise-polynomial space generated by \(b_{M_n}\).  Thus, by the exact Gram identity in \(\mathrm{def:corrected\mbox{-}moments}\),
\[
(\Pi_M u)(z)=b_{M_n}(z)^{\mathsf T}\int_{D_0}b_{M_n}(z')u(z')\,dz',
\qquad \|\Pi_Mu\|_2\le \|u\|_2.
\]
The projection is applied to each coordinate when \(u\) is vector-valued.

We first record the deterministic approximation facts used below.  If \(r>0\), \(m_r=\lceil r\rceil-1\), and \(u\in\mathcal H_d^r(L)\), restriction of \(u\) to a line segment followed by the one-dimensional Taylor formula gives, on every cube of side \(\ell\), a polynomial \(T\) of degree at most \(m_r\) satisfying
\[
\sup_x|u(x)-T(x)|\le C\ell^r.
\]
Indeed, the integral remainder is bounded by the stated order-\(m_r\) H\"older seminorm; when \(r\) is an integer, the exponent in the frozen definition is one and gives the same bound.  Applying this cell by cell after the change of variables \(x=hz\), and using the best-approximation property of \(\Pi_M\), yields
\[
\begin{split}
\|(I-\Pi_M)\{v_j(e(h\,\cdot)-3/8)\}\|_2&\le C\ell^\alpha,\\
\|(I-\Pi_M)\{v_j e(h\,\cdot)\}\|_2&\le C\ell^\alpha,\\
\|(I-\Pi_M)\{\mu_0(h\,\cdot)-1/2\}\|_2&\le C\ell^\beta.
\end{split} \tag{1}
\]
For the first two inequalities, multiply the cellwise Taylor polynomial of \(e\) by \(v_j\).  Its degree is at most \(m_\alpha+m_\gamma\le p_{\mathrm{deg}}\), so it belongs to the specified projection space.  For the third, \(m_\beta\le p_{\mathrm{deg}}\).  This proves (1) directly from \(\mathrm{ass:propensity\mbox{-}holder}\), \(\mathrm{ass:control\mbox{-}holder}\), and the definition of the two bases.

Write \(e_h(z)=e(hz)\), \(\tau_h^0(z)=\tau(hz)\), and define
\[
Q=\int_{D_0}v(z)v(z)^{\mathsf T}e_h(z)\{1-e_h(z)\}\,dz,
\qquad
R=\int_{D_0}v(z)e_h(z)\{1-e_h(z)\}\tau_h^0(z)\,dz.
\]
The propensity-envelope and propensity-normalization assumptions imply \(1/4\le e_h\le1/2\).  Since \(v\) is Lebesgue orthonormal,
\[
u^{\mathsf T}Qu\ge \frac{3}{16}\int_{D_0}\{u^{\mathsf T}v(z)\}^2dz
=\lambda_0\|u\|_2^2,
\qquad \lambda_0=3/16. \tag{2}
\]
Hence \(Q\) is invertible.  Put \(\theta=Q^{-1}R\) and \(\tau_h^\star(hz)=v(z)^{\mathsf T}\theta\).  The response-interiority assumption gives \(|\tau|\le3/4\); consequently (2), boundedness of \(e_h\) and \(v\), and the definition of \(R\) imply \(\|\theta\|_2\le C\).  The line-segment Taylor argument above supplies a polynomial \(t\) of degree at most \(m_\gamma\) with
\[
\sup_{z\in D_0}|t(z)-\tau(hz)|\le Ch^\gamma.
\]
If \(\theta_t\) is its coefficient vector in the \(v\)-basis, then (2), boundedness of the fixed-dimensional vector \(v\), and the normal equations give
\[
\|\theta-\theta_t\|_2
\le \|Q^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
\left\|\int_{D_0}v e_h(1-e_h)(\tau_h^0-t)\right\|_2
\le Ch^\gamma.
\]
Consequently
\[
\sup_{z\in D_0}|\tau_h^\star(hz)-\tau(hz)|\le Ch^\gamma,
\qquad
|v(0)^{\mathsf T}\theta-\tau(0)|\le Ch^\gamma. \tag{3}
\]

We next compute the population corrected moments rather than postulating their bias.  Put \(p=3/8\), \(\delta_e=e_h-p\), and \(\delta_\mu=\mu_0(h\,\cdot)-1/2\).  Conditional Bernoulli calculation gives
\[
\mathbb E[A(A-p)\mid X=hz]=e_h(z)(1-p),
\]
and
\[
\mathbb E[(Y-1/2)(A-p)\mid X=hz]
=\delta_e(z)\delta_\mu(z)+e_h(z)(1-p)\tau_h^0(z). \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, \(\mathbb E[A\mid X=hz]=e_h(z)\), \(\mathbb E[A-p\mid X=hz]=\delta_e(z)\), and
\[
\mathbb E[Y-1/2\mid X=hz]=\delta_\mu(z)+e_h(z)\tau_h^0(z). \tag{5}
\]
The exact uniform design, the factors \(h^{-d}\), independence for \(i\ne j\), and (4)--(5) therefore yield, with \(\overline Q=\mathbb E_P\widetilde Q_n\) and \(\overline R=\mathbb E_P\widetilde R_n\),
\[
\begin{split}
\overline Q
&=\int v v^{\mathsf T}e_h(1-p)
-\int \Pi_M(v\delta_e)e_hv^{\mathsf T},\\
\overline R
&=\int v\{\delta_e\delta_\mu+e_h(1-p)\tau_h^0\}
-\int \Pi_M(v\delta_e)\{\delta_\mu+e_h\tau_h^0\},
\end{split} \tag{6}
\]
where every unmarked integral in this proof is over \(D_0\).  Projection orthogonality changes the first difference in (6) into
\[
\overline Q-Q
=\int (I-\Pi_M)(v\delta_e)\,(I-\Pi_M)(e_hv)^{\mathsf T}.
\]
Thus (1) and Cauchy--Schwarz show
\[
\|\overline Q-Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C\ell^{2\alpha}. \tag{7}
\]
Let \(\Delta=\tau_h^0-v^{\mathsf T}\theta\).  Subtracting \(\overline Q\theta\) from \(\overline R\) in (6), adding and subtracting \(v\delta_e e_h\Delta\), and again using projection orthogonality gives the exact identity
\[
\overline R-\overline Q\theta
=\int (I-\Pi_M)(v\delta_e)(I-\Pi_M)(\delta_\mu+e_h\Delta)
+\int v e_h(1-e_h)\Delta. \tag{8}
\]
The last integral is zero by \(Q\theta=R\).  Equations (1), (3), projection contraction, and Cauchy--Schwarz now imply
\[
\|\overline R-\overline Q\theta\|_2
\le C\{\ell^{\alpha+\beta}+\ell^\alpha h^\gamma\}
\le C(\ell^S+h^\gamma). \tag{9}
\]

It remains to control sampling fluctuation.  Every coordinate of the empirical first-order terms has second moment at most \(Ch^{-d}\), because \(A,Y\) and the fixed-dimensional vector \(v\) are bounded and
\[
\int_{hD_0}h^{-2d}\,dx=h^{-d}.
\]
For the ordered pair terms, put \(k_M(z,z')=b_{M_n}(z)^{\mathsf T}b_{M_n}(z')\).  Orthonormality gives
\[
\int_{D_0}\int_{D_0}k_M(z,z')^2\,dz\,dz'=K. \tag{10}
\]
Hence a full two-index kernel has squared \(L^2\) norm at most \(CKh^{-2d}\).  Conditional integration over either one of its indices produces an orthogonal projection of one of the bounded functions in (4)--(5); projection contraction then bounds the squared \(L^2\) norm of every one-index projection by \(Ch^{-d}\).  Expanding the variance of the ordered sum makes terms with four distinct indices vanish by \(\mathrm{ass:iid\mbox{-}sampling}\).  There are at most \(Cn^3\) ordered pairs of kernels sharing one index and at most \(Cn^2\) sharing two.  Dividing by \(n^2(n-1)^2\), and using (10), proves
\[
\mathbb E_P\|\widetilde Q_n-\overline Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}^2
+\mathbb E_P\|\widetilde R_n-\overline R\|_2^2
\le C\left\{\frac1{nh^d}+\frac K{n^2h^{2d}}\right\}=:CV_n^2. \tag{11}
\]
The replacement of coordinatewise Euclidean norms by the operator norm costs only a constant because \(q\) is fixed.

Since \(\ell\to0\), (7) is at most \(\lambda_0/4\) for all \(n\ge n_0\), where \(n_0\) depends only on the fixed parameters.  On
\[
\mathcal E_n=\{\|\widetilde Q_n-\overline Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\lambda_0/4\},
\]
(2) and (7) imply \(s_{\min}(\widetilde Q_n)\ge\lambda_0/2\).  Thus the inverse branch of \(\mathrm{def:total\mbox{-}estimator}\) is used and \(\|\widetilde Q_n^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2/\lambda_0\).  Clipping cannot increase distance to \(\tau(0)\in[-3/4,3/4]\).  From (3), (9), and (11), Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\mathbb E_P[|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau(0)|\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_n}]
\le C\{h^\gamma+\ell^S+V_n\}. \tag{12}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_n^c\), both the clipped estimator and the target lie in \([-3/4,3/4]\).  Chebyshev's inequality and (11) give
\[
\mathbb E_P[|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau(0)|\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_n^c}]
\le \frac32\min\{1,CV_n^2\}\le CV_n. \tag{13}
\]
Combining (12)--(13), and enlarging the constant over the finitely many \(2\le n<n_0\), proves the advertised nonasymptotic envelope
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)}
\mathbb E_P|\widehat\tau_n(0)-\tau_P(0)|
\le C\left\{h_n^\gamma+\ell_n^S+(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}
+\frac{\sqrt{K_n}}{nh_n^d}\right\}. \tag{14}
\]
The finite enlargement is legitimate because \(n_0\) is fixed and the loss is at most \(3/2\).

Finally, \(S<S_\star<\gamma\), so \(x_n=n^{\eta(1/S-1/\gamma)}\ge1\) and
\[
x_n\le M_n=\lceil x_n\rceil\le2x_n,
\qquad
\tfrac12n^{-\eta/S}\le\ell_n\le n^{-\eta/S},
\qquad K_n\le Cn^{\eta d(1/S-1/\gamma)}. \tag{15}
\]
The definitions of \(\eta\) and \(h_n\) give
\[
h_n^\gamma=n^{-\eta},\qquad \ell_n^S\le n^{-\eta},
\qquad
\frac{\sqrt{K_n}}{nh_n^d}
\le Cn^{-1+\eta d/(2S)+\eta d/(2\gamma)}=Cn^{-\eta}. \tag{16}
\]
Also
\[
(nh_n^d)^{-1/2}\le n^{-\eta}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S\le\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}, \tag{17}
\]
which follows from \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\).  Substitution of (16)--(17) into (14) proves the claimed \(C\rho_n\) bound for every \(n\ge2\).  The half-open cells, finite sums, continuous singular values, measurable branch, matrix inversion on the nonsingular branch, and clipping also show directly that \(\widehat\tau_n(0)\) is a total finite Borel map, as required.

By the definitions of \(\eta\), \(S_\star\), and \(\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}\),
\[
\begin{split}
\eta<\frac{\gamma}{2\gamma+d}
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
1+\frac d{2\gamma}+\frac d{2S}>2+\frac d\gamma\\
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\frac d{2S}>1+\frac d{2\gamma}\\
&\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S<\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}=S_\star.
\end{split} \tag{44}
\]
Thus \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\) makes
\(\delta=\gamma/(2\gamma+d)-\eta\) strictly positive.  The two-sided conclusion of \(\mathrm{thm:sharp\mbox{-}exact\mbox{-}uniform\mbox{-}rate}\) then gives constants independent of \(n\) such that
\[
\frac{R_n}{\rho_n^{\mathrm{or}}}
\asymp\frac{n^{-\eta}}{n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}}
=n^\delta\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Hence no tuple in the stipulated strict below-elbow regime has the oracle order.  If one substitutes the boundary value \(S=S_\star\) into (44), equality holds, and both displayed powers are exactly \(n^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+d)}\).  Since both rate definitions are pure powers, this boundary equality introduces no logarithmic factor.

theorem.statement: For every \(n\ge2\), the construction \(\mathfrak H_n^{\mathrm{comp}}\) yields deterministic numbers \(0<\ell\le h\le1\), amplitudes \(a,b>0\), and two finite priors \(\Pi_+\) and \(\Pi_-\), supported on \(\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\), under each of which \(\tau_P(0)\) is constant, such that their constants differ by at least \(c\rho_n\) and the genuine fixed-\(n\) observed-data product mixtures have squared Hellinger distance at most \(1/4\).  More precisely, the singleton conditional sign-mixture laws are equal; if \(Q_{r,+}\) and \(Q_{r,-}\) denote the two conditional sign-mixture laws on any dependency component of size \(r\ge2\), then \[H^2(Q_{r,+},Q_{r,-})\le Ca^2b^2r^4(9/2)^r,\] and the full mixtures satisfy \[H^2\!\left(\int P_O^{\otimes n}\,d\Pi_+,\int P_O^{\otimes n}\,d\Pi_-\right)\le Cn^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2\le\frac14.\]  The construction keeps \(P_X\) exactly uniform on the full cube and uses neither an occupancy conditioning event nor Poissonization.
theorem.proof_tex:
Put \(p=3/8\).  We give the construction and prove every asserted property for the actual fixed-\(n\) experiment.

Define \(u(t)=e^{-1/t}\mathbf1\{t>0\}\),
\[
\chi(t)=\frac{u(1-t)}{u(1-t)+u(t-1/2)},
\qquad f(z)=\prod_{k=1}^d\chi(z_k).
\]
The denominator is positive for every \(t\), and direct differentiation at the flat endpoints shows that \(u\), hence \(\chi\) and \(f\), is \(C^\infty\).  Moreover, \(0\le f\le1\), \(f(0)=1\), and \(f(z)=0\) if any \(z_k\ge1\).  Likewise set
\[
\zeta(t)=e^{-1/(1-t^2)}\mathbf1\{|t|<1\}.
\]
This is a nonnegative \(C^\infty\) function supported on \([-1,1]\) and is bounded below by a positive constant on \([-1/2,1/2]\).

For \(0<\ell\le1\), let
\[
J_\ell=\{j\in\mathbb Z^d:\operatorname{dist}_\infty(\ell j,D_0)\le\ell\},
\quad
\phi_j(x)=\prod_{k=1}^d\zeta(x_k/\ell-j_k),
\quad
A_\ell(x)=\sum_{j\in J_\ell}\phi_j(x)^2,
\quad
\psi_j(x)=\frac{\phi_j(x)}{\sqrt{A_\ell(x)}}.
\]
The set \(J_\ell\) is finite.  For every \(x\in D_0\), coordinatewise nearest-integer rounding supplies \(j\in J_\ell\) with \(\|x/\ell-j\|_\infty\le1/2\).  Thus \(A_\ell\ge c_d>0\) on a neighborhood of \(D_0\).  At most \(3^d\) functions \(\phi_j\) are nonzero at a point.  The product and chain rules, applied inductively to \(A_\ell^{-1/2}\), therefore give, for every multi-index \(\nu\),
\[
\sum_j\psi_j(x)^2=1,\qquad
\operatorname{supp}(\psi_j)\subseteq\{x:\|x-\ell j\|_\infty\le\ell\},
\qquad
\|D^\nu\psi_j\|_\infty\le C_\nu\ell^{-|\nu|}. \tag{18}
\]
In particular, for independent Rademacher signs \(\vartheta=(\vartheta_j:j\in J_\ell)\),
\[
\left|\sum_j\vartheta_j\psi_j(x)\right|
\le \sqrt{3^d}\left(\sum_j\psi_j(x)^2\right)^{1/2}=:B. \tag{19}
\]

For \(0<\ell\le h\le1\), define
\[
f_h(x)=f(x/h),\qquad
F_\vartheta(x)=f_h(x)\sum_j\vartheta_j\psi_j(x),
\qquad K_h(x)=f_h(x)^2.
\]
Independence and centering of the signs and (18) imply, pointwise,
\[
\mathbb E_\vartheta F_\vartheta(x)=0,\qquad
\mathbb E_\vartheta F_\vartheta(x)^2=K_h(x),\qquad
|F_\vartheta(x)|\le B,\qquad 0\le K_h(x)\le1. \tag{20}
\]
For any fixed \(s>0\), put \(m=\lceil s\rceil-1\).  Product differentiation, (18), and \(\ell\le h\) bound every derivative through order \(m+1\) of \(F_\vartheta\) by \(C\ell^{-|\nu|}\), uniformly in \(\vartheta\), and every such derivative of \(K_h\) by \(Ch^{-|\nu|}\).  If \(D^mG\) denotes an order-\(m\) derivative, then
\[
|D^mG(x)-D^mG(y)|
\le C r^{-m}\min\{1,\|x-y\|_\infty/r\}
\le C r^{-s}\|x-y\|_\infty^{s-m}, \tag{21}
\]
with \(r=\ell\) for \(G=F_\vartheta\) and \(r=h\) for \(G=K_h\).  The first inequality uses respectively the sup-norm and the mean-value bound, and the second follows by splitting at \(\|x-y\|_\infty=r\).  It also covers integral \(s\), because then \(s-m=1\).  Consequently
\[
\|F_\vartheta\|_{\mathcal H_d^s(1)}\le C_s\ell^{-s},
\qquad
\|K_h\|_{\mathcal H_d^s(1)}\le C_sh^{-s}, \tag{22}
\]
where the notation in (22) means that every defining derivative bound and seminorm is bounded by the displayed right-hand side.

Choose fixed positive constants \(a_0,b_0\) so small that
\[
a_0B\le1/16,\qquad b_0\{B+a_0/p\}\le1/8. \tag{23}
\]
For amplitudes \(0<a\le a_0\), \(0<b\le b_0\), \(\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}\), and \(\vartheta\in\{-1,1\}^{J_\ell}\), define
\[
\begin{split}
e_\vartheta(x)&=p+aF_\vartheta(x),\\
\mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}(x)&=\frac12+\varepsilon bF_\vartheta(x)
+\frac{\varepsilon ab}{1-p}K_h(x),\\
\tau_\varepsilon(x)&=-\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p(1-p)}K_h(x),\\
\mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}(x)&=\frac12+\varepsilon bF_\vartheta(x)
-\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p}K_h(x).
\end{split} \tag{24}
\]
The last three lines satisfy \(\mu_{1,\varepsilon,\vartheta}-\mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}=\tau_\varepsilon\).  By (19) and (23), \(e_\vartheta\in[5/16,7/16]\) and both response means lie in \([3/8,5/8]\).

We now choose the deterministic scales.  With \(S=\alpha+\beta\), let
\[
\ell=c_\ell n^{-\eta/S},\qquad h=\ell^{S/\gamma},
\qquad a=c_a\ell^\alpha,\qquad b=c_b\ell^\beta, \tag{25}
\]
where \(0<c_\ell\le1\), \(0<c_a\le a_0\), and \(0<c_b\le b_0\) will be fixed below.  Since \(S<S_\star<\gamma\), \(0<\ell\le h\le1\).  Equations (22) and (25) show that the \(\alpha\)-H\"older size of \(4aF_\vartheta\) is at most \(Cc_a\), the \(\beta\)-H\"older size of \(bF_\vartheta\) is at most \(Cc_b\), and
\[
ab\|K_h\|_{\mathcal H_d^\beta(1)}
\le Cc_ac_b\ell^{S(1-\beta/\gamma)}\le Cc_ac_b,
\qquad
ab\|K_h\|_{\mathcal H_d^\gamma(1)}\le Cc_ac_b. \tag{26}
\]
Here \(\gamma>\beta\) is used in the first inequality.  Starting from the constants \(4p=3/2\) and \(1/2\), and then decreasing \(c_a,c_b\), (23), (26), and \(L\ge4\) prove
\[
4e_\vartheta\in\mathcal H_d^\alpha(L),\quad 1\le4e_\vartheta\le2,\quad
\mu_{0,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\in\mathcal H_d^\beta(L),\quad
\tau_\varepsilon\in\mathcal H_d^\gamma(L),\quad
1/8\le\mu_{a,\varepsilon,\vartheta}\le7/8. \tag{27}
\]

For each pair \((\varepsilon,\vartheta)\), construct a full-data law as follows.  Draw \(X\) uniformly on \(D_0\); conditional on \(X=x\), draw \(Y(0)\) and \(Y(1)\) independently with the two Bernoulli means in (24), draw \(A\) independently of them with success probability \(e_\vartheta(x)\), and set \(Y=AY(1)+(1-A)Y(0)\).  This law satisfies consistency and conditional exchangeability by construction, and all remaining member conditions of \(\mathrm{def:exact\mbox{-}model}\) follow from (24) and (27).  Thus every constructed law belongs to \(\mathcal P(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L)\).  Let \(\Pi_\varepsilon\) be the uniform prior on the finite set of these laws as \(\vartheta\) varies.  Since \(f_h(0)=K_h(0)=1\), its target is constant over the prior and equals
\[
\tau_\varepsilon(0)=-\frac{\varepsilon ab}{p(1-p)}. \tag{28}
\]

It remains to control the full product mixtures.  At a fixed \(x\), abbreviate \(F=F_\vartheta(x)\) and \(K=K_h(x)\).  For real \((s,t)\), replace \((a,\varepsilon b)\) in (24) by \((s,t)\).  In the cell order \((A,Y)=(1,1),(1,0),(0,1),(0,0)\), the four probabilities are
\[
\begin{split}
q_{11}(s,t)&=p/2+sF/2+ptF+st(F^2-K)-s^2tKF/p,\\
q_{10}(s,t)&=p/2+sF/2-ptF-st(F^2-K)+s^2tKF/p,\\
q_{01}(s,t)&=(1-p)/2-sF/2+(1-p)tF-st(F^2-K)-s^2tKF/(1-p),\\
q_{00}(s,t)&=(1-p)/2-sF/2-(1-p)tF+st(F^2-K)+s^2tKF/(1-p).
\end{split} \tag{29}
\]
Their sum is one.  By (20), for each cell \(z\),
\[
\mathbb E_\vartheta q_z(s,t;x)=q_{0,z},
\qquad q_0=(p/2,p/2,(1-p)/2,(1-p)/2). \tag{30}
\]
Thus the singleton conditional mixtures under \(t=b\) and \(t=-b\) are not merely close: both equal \(q_0\).

After decreasing \(a_0,b_0\) if necessary, (19), (23), and the generative form (24) ensure, throughout \(|s|\le a_0\), \(|t|\le b_0\),
\[
\frac12\le \frac{q_z(s,t;x)}{q_{0,z}}\le\frac32. \tag{31}
\]
Indeed, treatment probabilities then lie in \([5/16,7/16]\) and response means in \([3/8,5/8]\); direct comparison with \(q_0\) gives (31).  Formula (29), together with \(|F|\le B\) and \(0\le K\le1\), also bounds the first \(s\)-derivative, first \(t\)-derivative, and mixed \((s,t)\)-derivative of every ratio in (31) by a constant \(C_0\).

Fix arbitrary locations \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) whose active sign sets may overlap, and a cell vector \(z=(z_1,\ldots,z_r)\).  Relative to \(q_0^{\otimes r}\), the conditional mixture likelihood is
\[
M_r(s,t;z)=\mathbb E_\vartheta\prod_{i=1}^r
\frac{q_{z_i}(s,t;x_i)}{q_{0,z_i}}.
\]
The expectation is a finite sum.  Differentiating it, the product rule gives \(r\) terms in which both derivatives hit one factor and \(r(r-1)\) terms in which they hit two factors.  By (31) and the derivative bounds,
\[
|\partial_s\partial_tM_r(s,t;z)|\le C_1r^2(3/2)^r. \tag{32}
\]
At \(s=0\), replacing every sign \(\vartheta_j\) by \(-\vartheta_j\) replaces \(F_\vartheta\) by \(-F_\vartheta\) without changing its prior law.  Inspection of (29) gives \(M_r(0,b;z)=M_r(0,-b;z)\).  Two applications of the fundamental theorem of calculus and (32) yield
\[
|M_r(a,b;z)-M_r(a,-b;z)|
\le\int_0^a\int_{-b}^b|\partial_s\partial_tM_r(s,t;z)|\,dt\,ds
\le2C_1abr^2(3/2)^r. \tag{33}
\]
Both likelihoods in (33) are at least \(2^{-r}\) by (31).  Therefore
\[
\begin{split}
H^2(Q_{r,+},Q_{r,-})
&=\sum_zq_0^{\otimes r}(z)
\frac{|M_r(a,b;z)-M_r(a,-b;z)|^2}
{\{\sqrt{M_r(a,b;z)}+\sqrt{M_r(a,-b;z)}\}^2}\\
&\le Ca^2b^2r^4(9/2)^r. 
\end{split} \tag{34}
\]
For \(r=1\), (30) gives equality of the two laws and hence zero distance.

Condition now on the actual fixed vector \(X_{1:n}\).  Retain indices with \(f_h(X_i)\ne0\), and join \(i\) and \(j\) when \(\|X_i-X_j\|_\infty\le2\ell\).  If one sign \(\vartheta_k\) occurs in both \(F_\vartheta(X_i)\) and \(F_\vartheta(X_j)\), (18) implies this edge relation.  Hence distinct connected components depend on disjoint sets of independent signs.  Inactive observations have \(F_\vartheta=K_h=0\), and so have exactly the baseline cell law.  It follows, for the actual shared-sign prior, that the conditional product mixture factors over the graph components.

For probability laws \(P_j,Q_j\), their Hellinger affinities multiply under products.  Since \(H^2(P,Q)=2-2\int\sqrt{dP\,dQ}\), the elementary inequality \(1-\prod_jx_j\le\sum_j(1-x_j)\), \(0\le x_j\le1\), proves
\[
H^2\!\left(\bigotimes_jP_j,\bigotimes_jQ_j\right)
\le\sum_jH^2(P_j,Q_j). \tag{35}
\]
Let \(N_r\) be the number of graph components of size \(r\).  By (34)--(35), the conditional squared distance is at most
\[
Ca^2b^2\sum_{r=2}^nr^4(9/2)^rN_r. \tag{36}
\]

A component of size \(r\) is a connected labeled subset.  A connected graph contains a spanning tree.  Repeatedly delete the least-labeled leaf of a labeled tree and record its neighbor; the resulting word has length \(r-2\) over an alphabet of size \(r\).  Conversely, the multiplicity of each label in the word determines its current degree minus one, so repeatedly adjoining the least absent label reconstructs the unique deleted leaf and its incident edge.  This proves directly that there are \(r^{r-2}\) labeled trees.  For each such tree, integrate a root over the active set, which is contained in \([0,h]^d\), and then integrate every child over a sup-norm ball of radius \(2\ell\) about its parent.  Uniform independent design therefore gives
\[
\mathbb E N_r\le \binom nr r^{r-2}h^d(4\ell)^{d(r-1)}. \tag{37}
\]
No occupancy event has been imposed in (37).  Furthermore,
\[
\log(r!)=\sum_{k=1}^r\log k\ge\int_1^r\log x\,dx
=r\log r-r+1,
\]
so \(r!\ge(r/e)^r\).  With \(A=9/2\), (37) implies
\[
\mathbb E\sum_{r=2}^nr^4A^rN_r
\le nh^d\sum_{r=2}^nr^2(eA)^r(4^dn\ell^d)^{r-1}. \tag{38}
\]
If \(eA4^dn\ell^d\le1/2\), the series in (38) is at most \(Cn\ell^d\): factor out its first power of \(4^dn\ell^d\) and sum \(\sum_{r\ge2}r^2 2^{-(r-1)}<\infty\).  Hence (36)--(38) give
\[
\mathbb E_XH^2\{\mathsf M_+(\,\cdot\mid X_{1:n}),
\mathsf M_-(\,\cdot\mid X_{1:n})\}
\le Cn^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2. \tag{39}
\]
The two mixtures have the same uniform \(X_{1:n}\)-marginal.  Expanding the defining Hellinger integral therefore shows that their unconditional squared Hellinger distance is exactly the left side of (39).  This proves the requested fixed-\(n\) inequality directly, without Poissonization.

It remains only to fix the constants simultaneously.  From the definition of \(\eta\),
\[
1-\frac{d\eta}{S}<0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
S<\frac{d\gamma}{2\gamma+d}, \tag{40}
\]
so (25) and \(\mathrm{ass:below\mbox{-}elbow}\) give \(n\ell^d\le c_\ell^d\) for every \(n\ge2\).  Choose \(c_\ell>0\) sufficiently small to satisfy the series condition in (38).  Also
\[
n^2h^d\ell^da^2b^2
=c_a^2c_b^2n^2\ell^{2S+d+Sd/\gamma}
=c_a^2c_b^2c_\ell^{,2S+d+Sd/\gamma}, \tag{41}
\]
because \(\eta\{2+d/S+d/\gamma\}=2\).  Decrease the already fixed positive \(c_\ell\) once more so that the right side of (39) is at most \(1/4\).  This does not affect (27).  Finally, (28) gives the deterministic target separation
\[
|\tau_+(0)-\tau_-(0)|
=\frac{2ab}{p(1-p)}
=\frac{2c_ac_bc_\ell^S}{p(1-p)}n^{-\eta}
=c\rho_n,
\]
with \(c>0\).  All constants were chosen as functions only of the fixed parameter tuple.

For the requested early-kill tuple \(d=1\), \(\alpha=\beta=1/8\), \(\gamma=1\), one has \(S=1/4\), \(\eta=2/7\), \(\ell\asymp n^{-8/7}\), \(h\asymp n^{-2/7}\), and \(a=b\asymp n^{-1/7}\).  Thus \(n\ell\asymp n^{-1/7}\), singleton components vanish by (30), every \(r\ge2\) is included in (38), and \(n^2h\ell a^2b^2\asymp1\).  In particular, neither a singleton term nor a macro-scale leakage term survives.  This completes the certificate.
